title: Saving & Safety Net
description: Build the cushion that keeps one bad month from wrecking your year.
wolfLine: The pack survives winter because it planned in summer.

pay-yourself-first.definition: Moving money into savings as soon as you get paid, before you spend on anything else.
pay-yourself-first.example: Payday: $200 goes straight to savings, then you pay bills and live on the rest.

emergency-fund.definition: Cash you keep only for real surprises, like losing your job or an urgent repair.
emergency-fund.example: Your car breaks down and you need it for work. The emergency fund pays.

essential-expenses.definition: Your needs: the costs you must keep paying no matter what.
essential-expenses.example: Rent, food, bills, getting to work.

savings-account.definition: A bank account for money you're not planning to spend yet. The bank keeps it safe and pays you a little for holding it.

interest.definition: Extra money paid for using someone else's money. A bank pays you interest on savings. You pay interest when you borrow.
interest.example: Keep $1,000 in savings at 3% for a year and the bank adds $30.

high-yield-savings.definition: A savings account that pays more interest than a regular one, while keeping your money just as safe.
high-yield-savings.example: Regular account pays 0.5% a year. A high-yield one pays 4%.

liquid.definition: Easy to turn into cash quickly, without losing any of its value.
liquid.example: Money in a savings account is liquid. A house is not.

automatic-transfer.definition: A payment you set up once that moves money between accounts on a schedule, without you doing anything.
automatic-transfer.example: Every payday, $150 moves from your spending account to savings.

apy.definition: Annual percentage yield: what your savings earn in a year, counting the interest your interest earns.
apy.example: $5,000 at 4.00% APY earns about $200 in a year.

savings-goal.definition: A target with three parts: what it’s for, how much it costs, and when you need it.
savings-goal.example: $1,800 for a used scooter by June.

steps.title: Future you is counting on you
steps.body:
Saving means keeping some of today’s money for later. It turns a broken phone, a lost job or a surprise bill from a crisis into an annoyance.

It’s also how you pay for big things (a car, a trip, a deposit on an apartment) without borrowing.

steps.prompt: Your laptop dies. Which is the better place to be?
choices: Having $800 saved and buying a new one
Having nothing and borrowing at a high cost
steps.explain: Savings make it a shopping trip instead of a crisis.

steps.prompt: What kind of saving is it? Sort them.
items: A trip to Japan next year
Rent if you lose your job
A new bike in the spring
A vet bill you didn’t see coming
A deposit on your own apartment

steps.prompt: Saving $25 a week, how much do you have after a year of 52 weeks?
You need a big income before saving is worth it.
steps.explain: $25 a week is $1,300 a year. Starting small builds the habit.

steps.prompt: What’s the hardest part of saving for most people?
steps.explain: That’s why the next lessons are about making it automatic.

lessons.title: Pay Yourself First
lessons.summary: Savings come off the top, not out of the leftovers.

steps.context: To [[pay yourself first|pay-yourself-first]] means moving money into savings the moment you get paid, before you spend on anything else.
steps.prompt: It's payday. If you pay yourself first, what happens first?
choices: You wait to see what's left at month-end
steps.explain: Your savings get their cut before anything else touches the money.

steps.prompt: Saving whatever happens to be left at the end of the month works just as well.
steps.explain: There's rarely anything left. Take your cut first.

steps.context: 10% is the same as dividing by 10. 10% of $2,000 is $200.
steps.prompt: You take home $2,500 and pay yourself 10% first. How much goes to savings?
Paying yourself first only works if you earn a lot.
steps.explain: A small amount still builds the habit. Start at 1% if you have to.

steps.context: Can't manage 10%? Start at 5%, which is half of 10%, and raise it later.
steps.prompt: You save 5% of a $3,000 take-home. How much is that per month?
steps.explain: 10% of $3,000 is $300, and half of that is $150.

steps.prompt: At $150 a month, how much have you saved after a year (12 months)?
steps.explain: $150 × 12 = $1,800. From a habit you barely notice.

steps.prompt: When you pay yourself first, savings leave your account ___ you get paid.
steps.explain: Before you get a chance to spend it.

lessons.title: The Emergency Fund
lessons.summary: How much cushion you actually need.

steps.context: An [[emergency fund]] is cash you keep only for real surprises: losing your job, a medical bill, a car that breaks down.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a real emergency?
choices: A big sale on a TV
Your car breaks down and you need it for work
steps.explain: Unexpected, urgent and necessary. That's what the fund is for.

steps.context: A common goal is to save 3 to 6 months of [[essential expenses]]: the needs you must keep paying no matter what.
steps.prompt: Which of these is an essential expense?
steps.explain: Lose your job and rent is still due. Essential.

steps.context: Goal = essential expenses per month × number of months. $1,000 a month for 3 months = $3,000.
steps.prompt: Your essential expenses are $1,800 a month. How big is a 3-month emergency fund?
If you use your emergency fund, you should build it back up afterwards.
steps.explain: Refill the cushion before the next surprise.

steps.context: The bigger the risk of a bad month, the bigger the cushion you want.
steps.prompt: Who should aim for the bigger end, around 6 months?
choices: Someone whose pay changes a lot from month to month
Someone with a very steady job and no one relying on them
steps.explain: Less predictable income, thicker cushion.

steps.context: Six months of expenses sounds huge, so build it in steps. To see how long a goal takes, divide the goal by what you save each month.
steps.prompt: You save $300 a month toward a $3,600 emergency fund. How many months until you get there?

lessons.title: Dana’s Rainy Day
lessons.summary: A real emergency, a real fund, and what happens next.

story.title: The transmission
story.body:
Dana needs a car to get to patients’ homes. Last Tuesday the transmission failed. The repair: **$1,450**.

A few years ago that would have meant borrowing. This time Dana had an emergency fund of **$4,200**, built up at **$145** a month.

Dana’s essential expenses are **$1,900** a month.

steps.prompt: How much is left in the fund after the repair?
Was this a real emergency?
choices: Yes: Dana needs the car to earn a living
steps.explain: Unexpected, necessary and urgent. That’s exactly what the fund is for.

steps.prompt: Before the repair, how many full months of essential expenses did Dana have saved? Round down to whole months.
At $145 a month, how many months will it take to rebuild the $1,450?
What should Dana do now?
choices: Keep saving $145 a month until it’s back to $4,200
Stop saving, the emergency is over
Spend the rest on something fun
steps.explain: Refill the cushion before the next surprise.

steps.prompt: Using an emergency fund for an emergency means you failed.
steps.explain: That’s exactly what it’s for. Then you refill it.

lessons.title: Where to Keep It
lessons.summary: Safe, easy to reach, and earning something.

steps.context: A [[savings account]] is a bank account for money you're not planning to spend yet. The bank keeps it safe.
steps.prompt: What's a savings account for?
choices: Holding money you're not spending yet
steps.explain: Out of your everyday spending, but still yours.

steps.context: Banks pay you a little extra for keeping your money with them. That extra is called [[interest]].
steps.prompt: Your savings account adds a little extra money every year. What is that extra called?
steps.explain: The bank pays you for holding your cash.

steps.context: Interest is usually a yearly percentage. $1,000 at 3% earns $1,000 × 0.03 = $30 in a year.
steps.prompt: $10,000 sits in a savings account paying 4% a year. How much interest does it earn in one year?

steps.context: A [[high-yield savings account|high-yield-savings]] pays more interest than a regular one, and your money is just as safe.
steps.prompt: You have $10,000. A regular account pays 0.5% a year, a high-yield account pays 4%. Which earns more?
steps.explain: $400 a year versus $50. Same money, more growth.

steps.context: Money is [[liquid]] if you can turn it into cash quickly without losing any of it. Emergency money has to be liquid.
steps.prompt: Which of these is the most liquid?
choices: Money locked away for ten years
steps.explain: You can move it today, and it's all still there.

steps.prompt: Your emergency fund should be somewhere you can't touch it for years.
steps.explain: Emergencies don't wait. Keep it [[liquid]].

lessons.title: Watch It Grow
lessons.summary: Read a savings statement and see interest earning interest.

steps.context: Banks show savings rates as [[APY]], the annual percentage yield: what you’ll earn in a year, counting the interest your interest earns.
steps.prompt: What APY does this account pay?
steps.explain: It’s right at the top: 4.00%.

steps.prompt: Add up the four interest lines. How much did the account earn this year?
Without the statement: what’s 4% of $5,000?
steps.explain: $5,000 × 0.04 = $200. APY tells you the year’s total up front.

steps.prompt: Why does each interest line get a little bigger?
choices: Earlier interest is now earning interest too
steps.explain: Each quarter’s interest joins the balance, so the next quarter pays on a bigger number.

steps.prompt: Same $5,000 for a year. How much more does the 4.00% account earn than the 0.50% one?
Savings account rates can change over time.
steps.explain: Most savings rates move with the economy. Check yours once or twice a year.

lessons.title: Saving for a Goal
lessons.summary: What, how much, by when. Then divide.

steps.context: A [[savings goal]] has three parts: what it’s for, how much it costs, and when you need it.
steps.prompt: Which is a real savings goal?
choices: $1,800 for a used scooter by June
steps.explain: It has all three parts: what, how much and when.

steps.prompt: You need $1,800 in 9 months. How much a month?
You can only manage $150 a month. How many months will $1,800 take?
Two goals: $600 for a trip in 4 months, and $2,400 for a car in 24 months. You can save $250 a month. Which split works?
choices: $150 to the trip and $100 to the car
All $250 to the car, then the trip
why: The trip would get nothing before it’s due.
The trip would only reach $500 by month four.
steps.explain: $150 × 4 = $600 for the trip. $100 × 24 = $2,400 for the car. Both on time.

steps.prompt: Giving each goal its own savings bucket makes progress easier to see.
steps.explain: Many banks let you split savings into named pots for exactly this.

steps.prompt: Set up a goal. Put the steps in order.
items: Divide to get the monthly amount
steps.explain: What, how much, when, how much a month, then put it on autopilot.

lessons.title: Automate It
lessons.summary: Take willpower out of the equation.

steps.context: An [[automatic transfer]] moves money between your accounts on a schedule. You set it up once and it runs by itself.
steps.prompt: Why set up an automatic transfer to savings on payday?
steps.explain: Willpower runs out. Automation doesn't.

steps.prompt: Put a pay-yourself-first payday in order.
items: Your pay lands in your account
The automatic transfer moves savings out
steps.explain: Savings move before anything else touches the money.

steps.prompt: Automatic transfers work best when they happen right after payday.
steps.explain: Catch the money before you can spend it.

steps.context: Keep your savings in a **separate account** from your spending money. If you can't see it every day, you're less tempted to spend it.
steps.prompt: Why keep savings in a separate account?
choices: Mixing them is against the rules
So you're less tempted to spend it
steps.explain: Out of sight, out of reach.

steps.prompt: You automate $150 a week into savings. How much is that over a year (52 weeks)?
Your pay goes up by $200 a month. What's the smartest move?
choices: Stop saving now that you earn more
steps.explain: Save the raise before [[lifestyle creep]] finds it.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you're closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Saving
lessons.summary: Eight questions. Three strikes and you're out.

steps.prompt: Your car needs a surprise repair so you can get to work. What should pay for it?
steps.explain: Exactly what the [[emergency fund]] is for. Then rebuild it.

steps.prompt: Your essential expenses are $2,200 a month. How big is a 6-month emergency fund?
Emergency money should be liquid.
steps.explain: If you can't reach it fast, it can't save you.

steps.prompt: Moving money to savings before you spend anything is called paying yourself ___.
steps.explain: First cut is yours.

steps.prompt: $5,000 sits in a high-yield savings account paying 4% a year. How much interest does it earn in a year?
